demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I try to push them out of my mind

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be on guard all the time
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette: Rajinder Singh's eyes still scan the horizon with a mixture of habit and unease, even in his 80th year. As a retired Coast Guardsman, he spent decades surveying the waters for signs of danger, but one fateful incident has forever altered the way he views the world. It was during a routine rescue operation that Rajinder accidentally caused serious injury to another crew member. The specifics of what happened remain hazy in his mind - fragmented pieces of memory that refuse to cohere into a clear narrative. What he does recall, with vivid clarity, is the sound of sirens cutting through the air as they rushed to get medical help. Even now, when Rajinder hears sirens wailing in the distance, he feels an instinctual jolt of anxiety. He tries to push the memories out of his mind, telling himself that it wasn't really that bad or that it didn't happen at all - a coping strategy he's grown accustomed to over the years. Yet, the thoughts linger, festering like an open wound. The incident occurred in a natural setting not dissimilar from the quiet woods surrounding his current home. Whenever Rajinder ventures into these woods for a walk, he feels an overwhelming sense of unease, as if the trees themselves are closing in on him. He's taken to avoiding such excursions altogether, sticking instead to well-worn paths that offer a semblance of control. Rajinder has also grown increasingly leery of discussing plans for the future with his loved ones. Bringing up topics like travel or grandkids' graduations makes him acutely uncomfortable - as if he's tempting fate by even entertaining such thoughts. He'd much rather steer conversations toward safer, more nostalgic territory, reminiscing about his Coast Guard days or sharing stories from his late wife's life. Despite this attempt to insulate himself from potential dangers, Rajinder finds himself engaging in surprisingly reckless behavior when no one is looking. He'll take the stairs instead of the elevator or speed through intersections just as the lights are changing - tiny acts of defiance against an uncertain world that, paradoxically, leave him feeling more on edge. When he does venture out into public spaces, Rajinder always seeks out a seat in a corner or near an exit, mentally surveying his surroundings for potential escape routes. It's not just about physical safety; the sense of being 'on guard' has become second nature to him. This hypervigilance extends even to his relationship with himself - he often catches himself wondering if there's something fundamentally wrong with him as a person, some innate defect that led to the accident all those years ago. For Rajinder, recalling the event deliberately is akin to attempting to grasp a fistful of sand: the harder he tries, the more it slips through his fingers. But when memories do resurface unbidden - in dreams or during moments of quiet contemplation - they come flooding back with an unsettling vividness that feels almost too real. He's left reeling from these episodes, as if the past has momentarily invaded the present. As a widower living alone, Rajinder's grown increasingly isolated in recent years. His loved ones have encouraged him to seek help, sensing the darkness gathering around him like a shroud. It was only when he found himself lost on an unfamiliar street - and his subsequent panic response left him shaken - that Rajinder realized it was time to confront these festering wounds head-on. Now, as he begins therapy, he's not sure what the future holds or whether he'll ever find peace again; all he knows is that he can no longer continue living in this state of suspended animation, forever haunted by ghosts from his own past.
